headline.main: Trump's America: A Family Rent Asunder
headline.social: Trump's America: A Family Rent Asunder

intro: The father took part in the January 6 storming of the Capitol. His son turned him in to the FBI. Now that Donald Trump has pardoned him, Guy Reffitt and his wife are hoping for a return to normalcy - and fearful that it way never come.
text:
What he did, says the son, was terrible. And he would do it again.
He didn’t do anything wrong, says the father. He has no regrets.
Maybe, says the mother, everything will be okay again one day, with the family again sitting together under the Christmas tree or sharing a turkey dinner on Thanksgiving.
But it’s not going to be easy.
"I love my son,” says the mother. "And I stand by my husband.”
Father, mother, son and two daughters. This is the story of the Reffitt family from Texas.
And it’s also a story about America, this vast country that has the word "united” in its name. "E pluribus unum” – out of many, one – is the principle that formed this nation. But today, the U.S. is a divided country, completely at odds on fundamental issues. A place where the president and his supporters are in a hostile faceoff against those who did not vote for him. Where vengeance has been prioritized over cooperation.
A chasm runs through this country. And through the Reffitt family.
Sometimes, says Nicole Reffitt, the mother, it seems as though the chasm runs right through the kitchen, between the refrigerator and the island.
For some, Nicole is married to a hero and is the mother of a traitor.
For others, she is married to a terrorist and her son is the hero. She has learned to accept that, no matter from which side the remonstrations come. "I just take a deep breath and let it pass.”
What Happened?
In December 2020, Jackson Reffitt, who was 18 years old at the time, sent a warning to the FBI that his father, Guy Reffitt, 48, was stockpiling ammunition, gasoline and bear spray, and that he was making increasingly radical statements. On January 16, 2021, Guy Reffitt was arrested in the family home in Wylie, Texas, 10 days after he had been standing in his helmet and body armor in the middle of the crowd on the steps of the Capitol in Washington, D.C., shouting through a megaphone. He was a member of the Three Percenters, a right-wing extremist militia dedicated to fighting "government tyranny.”
Guy Reffitt was part of the mob that stormed the Capitol on January 6, 2021, in an attempt to prevent Congress from certifying Joe Biden’s election victory. A mob incited by the incumbent president, Donald Trump, who called on his supporters to "save our democracy.”
Trump refers to the attempted coup as a "day of love.” Immediately after being sworn in for his second term in the White House in January, he moved quickly to pardon the almost 1,300 men and women arrested and convicted in connection with the rioting.
Guy Reffitt says it was the "most consequential day in America’s recent history.” And, for him and his family at least, that is true.
The Father. Guy, 52:
It already feels like summer in mid-March in Texas. Guy Reffitt is sitting on a sofa in a small town south of Dallas, Nicole next to him. Between them is their gray-and-white poodle Oliver, who was with them back when everything was still okay. The Reffitts are currently staying at Guy’s sister’s place and taking care of her Siamese cats for as long as she is on vacation. They lost their own home when Guy was in prison and they could no longer pay their mortgage.
The usually now with their two daughters in Dallas. Peyton, 20, the younger of the two, has given them her room.
Guy Reffitt is rather small and slender – especially when compared to the man in the pictures depicting him as a convicted Capitol crusader.
When asked whether the years in prison changed him, he responds: "I lost weight.”
In summer 2022, Guy Reffitt was sentenced by a federal court in Washington D.C. to 87 months in prison, more than seven years, for trespassing on federal property with a firearm. Following the sentence, his wife Nicole could be seen standing in front of the courthouse flanked by her daughters. "We are patriots,” she said into the cameras, struggling to keep composure. "Trump deserves life in prison if my father is in prison for this long,” says her daughter Peyton.
The indictment also accused Guy Reffitt of obstruction of justice. The reference is to Jackson, his son, who testified against him.
"I never threatened Jackson,” says Guy. "He is my son.” He says that a statement he is alleged to have made to his son about traitors getting shot was taken out of context. His wife Nicole shakes her head next to him.
Their father never represented a danger to the family, both daughters said in testimony. It is a statement that would be confirmed by a judge as the trial progressed.
Ultimately, he spent four years and four days behind bars in nine different prisons, with 200 days in solitary confinement. The frequent moves are intentional, ensuring that the prisoner must get used to a new place over and over again. And it makes it difficult for the families to be with them.
Does he regret January 6?
"No. It was a political protest. We have the right to protest. We made it clear that things can’t keep going as they were.”
What can’t keep going?
"The government can’t just do as it likes.”
Guy Reffitt does not repeat the "Big Lie.” He doesn’t claim that the 2020 election was stolen.
But he also doesn’t say that Joe Biden and the Democrats won the election.
If the 2020 election was stolen, as Donald Trump and his supporters continue to insist, and which Guy Reffitt at least insinuates, then why did the Democrats, four years later, simply admit defeat without a peep? The Democratic candidate, Kamala Harris, congratulated Donald Trump and Joe Biden invited him to the White House after the election victory.
"Trump’s victory was too decisive this time. He even got the popular vote,” says Reffitt. And he’s right: Trump received more votes than Harris.
"I don’t think the election was stolen, but there was a lot of maneuvering,” says Nicole Reffitt.
Is that a good enough reason to storm the Capitol?
Reffitt says he was as surprised as anyone to suddenly find himself on the steps of the Capitol, megaphone in his belt. He says he didn’t have to cross any barriers – there was nothing there. No fences. No bollards. Just a lot of people with whom he had marched to the front of the Capitol from the rally Trump had held on the Ellipse.
There is video footage of him standing on the steps. Reffitt is holding a bottle of water and is being fired on with pepper balls by a police officer.
Guy Reffitt, prosecutors said, "lit the match” that incited the mob to break down the doors and storm into the building.
Was that day worth four years in prison? Was it worth the rupture in his own family?
"I am to blame for what happened to my family. That is something I deeply regret,” says Reffitt. He says he bears the responsibility and wants to make amends.
A tattoo on his right forearm reads 376782-C2B, his prisoner number. On his other are the initials of his three children: S for Sarah, J for Jackson and P for Peyton.
"The things you do in prison,” he says with a short laugh.
Guy Reffitt used to earn a six-figure salary working for oil companies like Saudi Aramco and the Kuwait Oil Company. The family lived on the island of Penang in Malaysia for four years, spending time on the beach, taking vacations in Thailand and sending their children to private schools. But in 2016, the price of oil collapsed and Guy lost his job. The family moved back to Texas, and instead of work, Guy Reffitt’s life became filled by Donald Trump, served up by Fox News and Newsmax, echo chambers where reality only makes periodic appearances. Trump first became a presidential candidate and then he was elected. Guy liked how he talks and what was saying. And what he promised: to make America great again.
In Guy Reffitt’s telling, it sounds like he is also referring to himself. He joined the right-wing militia Three Percenters.
During this period, the family sometimes didn’t even have enough money for gas.
Sarah, the eldest, wanted to go to college. But instead, she started taking even more shifts as a waitress. They all put their money together.
When the coronavirus brought everyday life and public activities to a screeching halt in spring 2020, the extremes began emerging.
Guy, who was 48 years old at the time, went from being a fan of Trump to being an apostle.
"Dad became something like an extension of Donald Trump,” says Sarah Reffitt, 27, sitting on a barstool in the Lazy Dog, the restaurant in northern Dallas where she works as a manager and where her younger sister Peyton waits tables. Quite some time passed before she responded to an interview request. She is actually rather tired of talking about it all. Ultimately, though, she assented and – like her mother, father and brother – she spoke openly and thoughtfully.
Jackson, 18 at the time, had been on the liberal side of the spectrum for quite some time and was further politicized by the death of George Floyd, a Black man killed by a white policeman. Guy was constantly wearing his MAGA cap while Jackson sported T-shirts with slogans like "Trans Lives Matter.” And when the pandemic arrived, they were no longer just arguing about secure borders, immigration and the police, but also about masks and vaccination.
In response to Trump’s loss in the fall 2020 election, Guy Reffitt hung an American flag in the living room. As a memorial.
The debates were no longer about differences of opinion or diverging approaches. They were about what was true and what was false. Guy began speaking about wanting to go to the nation’s capital. And he ordered ammunition, a GPS tracker, gasoline and bear spray.
During this period, he was convinced that the electricity would soon fail. It was, he believed, part of the plot to cover up the election fraud. On January 5, he set off for Washington.
One of the two Siamese cats starts mewing like a baby. Guy picks it up and begins petting it on his lap on the sofa.
Guy Reffitt didn’t hurt anybody on January 6. He didn’t attack any police officers and entered the Capitol for the first time in his life just this February, as part of a tour he took with Nicole. A selfie shows the two of them wearing an audio guide in the National Statuary Hall, smiles on their faces.
The judiciary, he believes, wanted to make an example of him – and of many of the "J6ers.”
"Hostages” is the word Trump used to describe those convicted for their activities on January 6.
In prison, Reffitt read the Federalist Papers – all 85 of them – to gain a better understanding of the ideas out of which the Constitution arose.
Lawfare is a term used to describe using the judiciary to wage war. Instrumentalizing laws to, for example, target one’s opponents. Donald Trump and his followers used the term when a court in New York found Trump guilty on 34 counts in May 2024. A verdict to which Guy Reffitt responded by sending his wife Nicole a text message reading: "DJT is now one of us.”
These days, the term is primarily used in reference to Donald Trump’s remolding of the state to suit his needs. To the way in which he has installed his loyalists in all of the most powerful positions and the courses they have now charted – at his behest – at the FBI and the Justice Department.
When Teslas are lit on fire, the cars produced by his henchman-in-chief Elon Musk, the attorney general steps before the cameras to declare it domestic terrorism.
Those who don’t suit Trump must go. He is currently in the process of doing away with the Department of Education, a hotbed of hostility in his eyes. More than 1,000 civil servants have lost their jobs.
Guy Reffitt’s voice grows flinty. He says he has no sympathy for anyone who is fired. He also lost his job, he says, and then everything else. "I was stuck in a box. I had to walk in chains and shackles for four years.”
"If all you’ve lost is your job, stop whining!”
For Guy Reffitt, it is Donald Trump who is now putting democracy back on the right track. Fixing it. He is the one who is again taking the Constitution seriously – and the will of the Americans.
That, says Guy Reffitt, is what January 6, 2021, was all about.
Trump’s election victory has now belatedly lent significance to the years he spent in prison.
The Son. Jackson, 22:
He gets in touch over video call. It’s not possible to meet him in person and he declines to reveal his location.
He has long, curly hair and his balanced facial features were clearly inherited from his mother. He is sitting at a desk, a cat strolling through the picture here too.
When he thinks of his father, says Jackson Reffitt, his overriding emotion is one of emptiness.
The last time they spoke, Guy Reffitt was still in prison and the call broke off every 15 minutes, forcing him to redial. Jackson tried to tell his father why he was afraid.
Liar, came the reply.
His parents have continued to radicalize over the last several years, says Jackson – his father in prison and his mother as a result of what she has been through.
"She used to be pretty liberal, very open,” he says, describing his mother.
He remembers that she once asked him if he was gay. "No idea,” he answered. "It makes no difference, anyway,” she then said. He says he really loves his parents, but that makes everything all the more difficult.
"We haven’t reached this point because of me, but because of all these awful people, these evil thoughts they are surrounded by.” Their love changes nothing about the fact that both his parents belong to the alt-right and their son is a liberal. That his views are diametrically opposed to theirs – on pretty much everything.
He swallows hard and then lets out a little laugh. It’s a bitter realization: His parents believe his is part of a dangerous cult – and he thinks the same about them. In one argument, his father called him a "government puppet."
Despite all that, it was Guy who made sure that Jackson registered to vote when he turned 18. He got him the papers and told him: "Vote for the right one.”
"He knew, of course, that I wouldn’t.”
"What I did was really bad,” says Jackson Reffitt, adding that he’s not proud of having turned his father in to the FBI.
It was Christmas Eve 2020. Guy Reffitt had repeatedly talked about going to Washington. "Something big” has to happen to "prevent tyranny,” he wrote in the family chat. Then there were the weapons and the ammunition. The full gas canisters in the garage.
"I didn’t want anything to happen to anyone. I didn’t want that responsibility,” he says. Jackson opened tips.fbi.gov and reported his father Guy.
Maybe he was paranoid, he says, but he was afraid. He had the feeling that he had to tell someone.
It was a feeling that had grown over the course of several weeks.
One time, Nicole came into his room and sat down on his bed, telling him that she was worried about Guy. At the time, he was driving across the entire state of Texas to go to militia meetings, once even driving seven hours to Mississippi to conduct surveillance on a Black Lives Matter activist. He also took over responsibility for conducting security checks on new members of the Three Percenters.
Today, Guy Reffitt says that he was a "bit too emotional” during this period.
Nicole says that she was just happy that he had something to do.
Jackson says that his father was so wound up in his right-wing extremist fantasies that he could no longer think clearly. He was so angry. Once, he says, Guy ran to the door with his loaded AR-15, a semi-automatic assault rifle, because he had heard a noise.
The FBI finally got in touch with Jackson on January 6. And 10 days later, a SWAT team surrounded the Reffitt home and led Guy away.
For some, Jackson is a traitor. For others, he is a hero.
In an interview a few days after his father’s arrest, a CNN journalist praised his courage and his sense of civic responsibility. Even his dentist told him he had done the right thing.
Jackson hates being told such things, it embarrasses him. "It’s not a great feeling to betray your own father.”
A comment beneath the CNN story reads: "You are a pathetic piece of shit.”
After the interview, his mother sent him a text message: "I love you. Don't forget - and don’t read the comments!”
Jackson then moved out to a shared apartment. One time, Nicole showed up at his door late at night. She was drunk, he says, and started screaming at him.
"Finally, she was honest and she was telling me,” he says. "It was good.”
Good moments, though, were few and far between.
He feels lonely, says Jackson. He has his boyfriend, but he misses his family. He takes shifts in the restaurant where he works on holidays, and he spent his 22nd birthday crying in his car, he says.
On the evening of November 5, 2024, after the polls had closed and it was clear that Donald Trump had won a second term, Jackson Reffitt bought a weapon.
"I’m not afraid of my father,” he says – Guy, at the time, was still locked away in a cell in Oklahoma. But he is afraid of "the violent people who surround” his father.
Jackson saw on the news that on his very first day in office, Donald Trump fulfilled his campaign promise and pardoned those who had been convicted in connection with January 6. More than 1,000 people, including those who had committed violent crimes – a group that his vice president, JD Vance, had said a short time before shouldn’t be let free.
The first image that Jackson Reffitt saw of his newly freed father was in his mother’s X feed. It showed Guy Reffitt in the kitchen having a drink with Stewart Rhodes, the founder of the right-wing extremist militia Oath Keepers. He had been sentenced to 18 years without the possibility of parole before Trump freed him as well.
Jackson Reffitt decided to move again. He wanted to make sure that no one in his family knew where he lives.
The Mother. Nicole, 52:
She sometimes calls him Queenie. Guy, she says, is a drama queen.
They first met at high school in Martinsville, Texas. Guy wore leather and long hair, Nicole was the cool blonde with perfectly balanced facial features. They got married in Las Vegas. When she introduced Guy to her grandmother, he told her that he stayed out of politics and that he didn’t vote because it didn’t matter anyway. Nicole’s grandmother responded: "Then you have nothing to say here either.” Only those who vote, she said, could share their opinions.
Guy Reffitt now knows that votes do, in fact, matter. They gave him his freedom back.
Nicole Reffitt spent 17 years as a stay-at-home mother. When Guy lost his job, she started working in a department store as a saleswoman, work that she quite enjoyed, in part because she was good at it. In contrast to Guy, she became political early on. She read the works of founding father Thomas Paine and of the Republican Rand Paul. She is not the kind of person to say something just because she heard it somewhere. She was on the libertarian wing of the Republican party, very Texan. And not a Trump fan girl. She found Trump too vulgar.
She only became an activist when her husband was locked away in prison.
She says she used to believe in the rule of law. Before her husband’s trial. In the courtroom, it was called "The United States vs Guy Wesley Reffitt” – us against the most powerful government in the world, Nicole thought to herself. She sometimes had trouble breathing.
Guy Reffitt pleaded "not guilty.” And was sentenced to 87 months. Had he pleaded guilty and accepted a plea deal, his sentence would almost certainly have been far shorter.
Nicole Reffitt left Texas, and her two daughters, for Washington, D.C., moving into a white house in the Capitol Hill neighborhood with other J6 family members. It was more than just a home-sharing arrangement, it was a community of the like-minded.
She would wear a "Make America Great Again” hat as she walked through the city and held vigils in front of the prison – every evening. Trump supporters aren’t particularly welcome in Capitol Hill and Nicole was yelled at on occasion. Once, somebody spit on the ground in front of her.
She frequently attended court hearings, and not just those of her husband. She took a seminar at the right-wing Heritage Foundation.
Back home, her older daughter Sarah took care of the younger Peyton. She started having anxiety attacks and had to change schools.
Today, Sarah says: "It was all a bit too much.”
When the family could no longer afford the mortgage on their house, the daughters moved into a rented apartment. Nicole flew to Dallas to pack the boxes.
"I was mourning the life that we used to have – even though my husband was still alive. I was mourning my son, even though he was also still alive. It was almost impossible to find joy in anything.”
In a restaurant in Washington, she was refused service because she was wearing her MAGA hat. The name of the place? As You Are.
"That was our fight,” she says. To demonstrate openly – even in a city like Washington, D.C., which is almost completely Democratic – on which side she stood.
Sometimes, with the fight now over, she finds herself wondering what she should do next.
Did they win?
"I am happy that Trump won the election. That Guy is now free,” she says.
Has she lost her son?
"I don’t know.”
On January 6, 2025, Donald Trump called Nicole and the other family members of those convicted for storming the Capitol. In their house on Capitol Hill, they put the phone on loudspeaker. "Keep your chin up, I love you,” Trump told them. And that he was going to pardon their husbands.
Nicole Reffitt was never in favor of a blanket pardon for all J6ers. "There were dangerous people among them,” she says. Five people died in the turmoil. For several months afterwards, the National Guard cordoned off streets around the Capitol.
Nicole says she is saddened by the discord.
Within just a few days in January, both her husband and her son were gone. Their extended family is deeply divided. One part no longer speaks with Jackson because they see him as a traitor who delivered his father into the hands of the political enemy. The other part no longer speaks with Guy and her. They want nothing to do with the storming of the Capitol, with prison.
Guy Reffitt is talking about how the FBI was instrumentalized under Democratic presidents like Barack Obama and Joe Biden and how agents infiltrated social media platforms to incite "hatred of conservatives.” When he moves on to how the education system systematically took his son from him through liberal teachers and progressive indoctrination, Nicole Reffitt lays her hand gently on his knee and goes outside for a smoke.
When she returns, she says: "Maybe we can say that the FBI instrumentalized our son, so we don’t have to blame Jackson.”
She sometimes wants to simply forget that her son recorded conversations he had with his father – in the kitchen, in the living room. And that he forwarded chats and audio files to the FBI.
She also thinks it’s okay to sometimes be furious with her son.
She can be angry with him, she says, but others cannot be.
There is that one incident that the family cannot agree on. Guy Reffitt asked Jackson about his political convictions, and Jackson responded by saying he was communist. And that America should be communist.
"That makes you a traitor, bro,” Guy purportedly said. And traitors deserve to be shot.
Guy Reffitt denies having said such a thing.
"He says that because he is afraid of you,” says Nicole.
"He says that because he’s been indoctrinated,” says Guy.
We should leave him alone, Nicole says. Be patient and wait for him to get in touch of his own accord.
They are proud of the fact that Jackson is the way he is. That he has his own views and acts on them.
"That’s how we raised him,” says Guy.
Sometimes, Nicole is afraid that Jackson has already distanced himself too much from them.
Guy is going to start working again soon, first for his brother, an engineer who repairs cellphone towers.
Nicole Reffitt says she is afraid of the future. They are trying their best to find their way back to normalcy. To life.
And maybe things will turn out okay at some point. She has, in any case, regained her ability to find joy in things.
"There's a lot of love for my family,” she says. But she has thus far been unable to rediscover the lightness.
"My southern belle,” says Guy. Sometimes, he is surprised by her anger. She was never like that before.
There is an off-Broadway play that portrays what happened to their family. It’s called "Fatherland.” At some point, they want to travel to New York to watch it. An invitation has not been forthcoming.
A Country Reflected in a Family
"Our family is like a miniature version of the country,” says Guy Reffitt. He still believes that Jackson will return one day and heal the wound.
Guy is convinced. Nicole is merely hopeful.
She wants to be part of Jackson’s life. She wants to cook for him, and comfort him when he needs it.
"I won’t let him go. I’m his mother.”
"I love you Jackson,” Guy Reffitt said directly into the camera after being released from prison.
"I don’t think he’s going to change his views and suddenly join our side,” says Nicole.
Nor does he have to, says Guy. "We just won’t talk about politics.” He wants everything to go back to how it used to be: eating together, going swimming together. There shouldn’t be this hatred, says Guy. "Not in our family, not in our country. It’s just crap.”
Sometimes, he just has to laugh out loud because everything is so messed up.
